summary: Palestine has no border control of its own — every route into the West Bank runs through Israeli-controlled crossings (Ben Gurion Airport or the Allenby Bridge from Jordan), so Israel's entry rules determine who gets in; the Palestinian Authority issues no visas, and Gaza is effectively closed to travelers.

passportValidity.text: Israeli border authorities, who control all crossings into the West Bank, require a passport valid for at least 6 months on arrival.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine

travelInsurance.text: Not required for entry, but check carefully that your policy covers the Palestinian territories — many insurers exclude them or follow government travel advisories.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine

onwardTicket.text: Israeli border officials expect a return or onward ticket and may ask detailed questions about your itinerary, accommodation and contacts.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine

proofOfFunds.text: No fixed amount is published; Israeli border officers may ask about your means and the purpose of your visit.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine

currencyLimits.text: Israeli rules apply at all crossings — cash of ILS 50,000 or more (or the equivalent) must be reported on entry.

source.name: Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Expatriates of the State of Palestine

notes: Customs on entry are handled by Israeli authorities at Ben Gurion Airport or the Allenby (King Hussein) Bridge, so Israeli import rules apply.
Israel issues a paper entry slip rather than stamping passports. Keep it, as it is checked at hotels and checkpoints.

payments.text: The Israeli shekel is the everyday currency in the West Bank, with Jordanian dinars and US dollars accepted for larger purchases; cards work in city hotels, restaurants and larger shops, but markets and shared taxis run on cash.

safety.text: Conditions differ sharply by area: Gaza is a war zone and closed to travelers, while the West Bank sees checkpoints, periodic military operations, settler violence and protests. Most governments advise against all travel to Gaza and urge heightened caution — or advise against travel — for parts of the West Bank. Check your government's advice and local conditions daily.

source.name: UK FCDO — travel advice for the Occupied Palestinian Territories

bestTimeToVisit.text: Spring and fall offer mild weather for Bethlehem, Ramallah, Jericho and hiking in the hills; summers are hot and midwinter can be cold and wet in the highlands.

idp.text: Palestine is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties
source.instrument: Convention on Road Traffic, Vienna, 8 November 1968 (UNTS vol. 1042, p. 17)

driving.text: Palestine is a party to the 1968 Vienna Convention on Road Traffic but not to the 1949 Geneva one, so the International Driving Permit it is bound to recognize is the 1968 Vienna version. A permit issued under the 1949 Geneva Convention carries no treaty obligation here. Whether a permit is required in addition to a national license, and for how long a foreign license may be used, are set by national road law and have not been checked for Palestine yet.

source.name: UN Treaty Collection — Convention on Road Traffic (Vienna, 1968), status of parties

tips.text: There is no Palestinian visa. Entry is governed entirely by Israel. Travelers reach the West Bank through Ben Gurion Airport or the Allenby (King Hussein) Bridge from Jordan, passing Israeli immigration in both cases.

Israeli border officers may question travelers heading to the West Bank at length about their itinerary and contacts — answer factually and allow extra time. Admission is at Israel's discretion and can be refused.
Gaza is closed to travelers — the Rafah crossing with Egypt operates only intermittently for aid and specific categories of people, not tourism.
Movement within the West Bank passes through Israeli checkpoints. Carry your passport and entry slip at all times and expect delays, especially around Jerusalem.
Security conditions can deteriorate with little warning. Register with your embassy where possible and monitor its advice throughout your trip.

faq.question: Do I need a visa to visit Palestine?
faq.answer: The Palestinian Authority issues no visas and operates no border control, so entry is governed by Israel's rules. Nationalities that are visa-exempt for Israel — the EU, US, UK, Canada, Australia and many others — need Israel's ETA-IL electronic travel authorization before flying; other nationalities need an Israeli visa from an embassy. Whatever admits you into Israel also covers onward travel to most of the West Bank.

faq.question: How do I get to the West Bank?
faq.answer: Either fly into Israel's Ben Gurion Airport and travel overland (Ramallah and Bethlehem are under an hour from Jerusalem), or cross from Jordan over the Allenby (King Hussein) Bridge. Both routes pass Israeli border control. There is no airport in the Palestinian territories.

faq.question: Can tourists visit Gaza?
faq.answer: No. Gaza is closed to travelers: the Erez crossing from Israel is shut to visitors and the Rafah crossing from Egypt operates only intermittently for humanitarian and other approved categories. All governments advise against any attempt to enter.

faq.question: Can Israeli citizens visit Palestinian cities?
faq.answer: Israeli law bars Israeli citizens from entering Area A — the parts of the West Bank under full Palestinian Authority control, including central Ramallah, Nablus, Jericho and Bethlehem — with red warning signs posted at the entrances. Gaza is closed to entry entirely.

faq.question: Will visiting the West Bank leave a stamp in my passport?
faq.answer: Normally no. Israel issues a paper entry slip instead of stamping passports, and the Palestinian Authority adds no stamps of its own. Be aware that some Arab and Muslim-majority countries treat any other evidence of travel through Israel as grounds for refusing entry.
